newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIA MINERAL SEARCH SATELLITE PROJECT PLANNED.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIA MINERAL SEARCH SATELLITE PROJECT PLANNED.

text.p: A plan to launch an Australian satellite which can spot mineral-rich regions around the globe has passed a feasibility study, project partners said on Monday.

The ARIES-1 (Australian Resources Information and Environment Satellite) project has been developed by government scientific research body CSIRO, the Australian Centre for Remote Sensing (ACRES) and Auspace, a unit of joint venture aerospace group, Matra-Marconi.

"The study confirmed commercial and technical feasibility of the project and concluded the specifications of the system will meet customer requirements," the partners said in a statement. The partners said construction of the satellite is expected to start before the end of 1997 for launch in 2000.

Project scientist Jon Huntington from CSIRO's exploration and mining unit said the satellite would have a four year lead on its nearest rivals and offered a leap in technology compared to existing Landsat and SPOT satellites.

"The satellites (imaging spectrometer) instrument will be able to diffentiate between the spectral signatures of various minerals in the rocks and soil even through moderate vegetation cover," Huntington told a luncheon.
The satellite, which could differentiate between some vegetation species and environmental indicators, would also be able to monitor environmental conditions around the globe, Huntington said.
Huntington said satellite imaging had large advantages over fixed wing aircraft which were restricted in their movements by national borders, terrain logistics and weather conditions.

Auspace managing director Ted Stapinski told the lunch that once launched into low orbit, the satellite would circle the earth from north to south every 90 minutes and would be able to examine any region once every six to seven days.
"When the satellite is not being used to image specific areas for customers we will be building an image archive of the whole world which should take about five years to complete," Stapinski said.
He said the satellite had about a five year life but the partners expected to have a more advanced satellite, ARIES-2, in development phase by the time ARIES-1 expired.
The project is expected to cost in excess of A$200 million and funding is being arranged through the project's finance adviser, Macquarie Bank Ltd.
In a separate statement, Macquarie said it hoped to fund the project through debt and equity sourced from resource companies which would participate in an unincorporated joint venture.
Macquarie said it envisaged a funding package would be put together by the end of 1997 with equity participants contributing a minimum of A$10 million to the project.
